summary: This informational memo describes version 2 of the Internet Cache Protocol as implemented in two web proxy cache packages, which lets caches ask their neighbors whether they hold a copy of an object.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Cache Protocol (ICP) lets one web cache ask another whether a URL is available there. This memo defines the messages used for those questions and replies, not the cache-selection process itself.

questions: what is the internet cache protocol
subtitle: The version 2 message format caches use to ask neighbors about URLs.

tldr.problem: A web cache needs a quick way to ask neighboring caches whether they have a requested URL before choosing where to retrieve it.
tldr.mechanism: ICP defines a message header and opcodes for queries and replies such as HIT, MISS, DENIED and MISS_NOFETCH. In current practice it commonly runs over UDP, though the RFC does not require UDP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2186 records the format and fields of ICP version 2. Its companion RFC 2187 describes how to apply ICP to web caches.

today: RFC 2186 is an Informational memo describing ICP version 2. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it; the memo points to RFC 2187 for ICP's application to web caches.

sections.title: Cache Queries and Replies
sections.content:
The Internet Cache Protocol (ICP) is a lightweight message format for communication between web caches. Caches use HTTP to transfer objects, but ICP can provide quick hints about whether a neighboring cache has a URL. A query receives a reply such as HIT or MISS.

The RFC says ICP is implemented over UDP in current practice, but is not limited to UDP. A cache needs to make its choice quickly, often within a second or two, so a missing reply may indicate that the neighbor or network path is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache can ask nearby caches whether they have a URL before requesting the object. ICP is designed for a quick answer, but the memo does not require a specific transport protocol.

sections.title: The ICP Message Header
sections.content:
An ICP message contains a fixed header of 20 octets followed by a variable-size payload. Fields use network byte order, and the total message length must not exceed 16,384 octets. The header carries an opcode, version, length, request number, options, option data and sender host address.

The request number is copied into the reply. The sender host address is an IPv4 address, but the RFC says it is not used in practice and should probably not be trusted over information supplied by the network socket. Most payloads contain a null-terminated URL.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a fixed set of fields that identifies its type, length and request. The rest usually carries the URL being checked.

sections.title: Queries, Replies and Echoes
sections.content:
A query includes the URL and a requester address, which identifies the cache's client and may be zero when unspecified. The reply copies the request number and URL. HIT means the object is available; MISS means it is absent; MISS_NOFETCH means the cache is up but asks the requester not to fetch the object from it now.

Other replies indicate an error, denied access or a hit that includes the object itself. The RFC does not recommend HIT_OBJ because it bypasses HTTP authorization and age checks and may cause UDP fragmentation. SECHO and DECHO can probe an origin server or a cache that does not use ICP.
sections.plainLanguage: A neighbor can report a hit, a miss, a processing error or denied access. A miss marked NOFETCH tells the requester not to fetch the object from that cache at that time.

sections.title: Optional Query Flags
sections.content:
The ICP_FLAG_HIT_OBJ option says that the requester can accept an object included in a HIT_OBJ reply. The RFC still advises against using that reply type because it bypasses normal HTTP processing and can create large datagrams.

ICP_FLAG_SRC_RTT asks the responding cache to include its measured round-trip time to the origin server. If the measurement is available, it is returned as a 16-bit millisecond value in option data. The reply must not be delayed while waiting for a measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: A query can allow the cache to include the object or ask for a round-trip-time measurement. The cache should answer without waiting for a measurement it does not already have.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC refers readers to RFC 2187 for security issues relating to ICP. It also cautions that the sender address field in an ICP message should probably not be trusted over the address reported by the receiving socket.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo directs readers to RFC 2187 for ICP security issues. It also warns implementers not to rely on the sender address written inside the message.

fields.name: Sender Host Address
fields.desc: IPv4 sender address; not used in practice.
